title: Review 2: Satins, ribs, twill derivatives and drafting

quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: Names of weaves and of the drawings that describe them.

questions.q: In a satin weave each warp end is
options: Up on only one pick of the repeat
Down on only one pick of the repeat
questions.explain: Satin is warp-faced: the end floats over all the picks but one. Sateen is the weft-faced opposite.

questions.q: The move number of a satin is
options: How many ends the interlacing point shifts on each successive pick
questions.explain: It scatters the single interlacings so that no two touch.

questions.q: A weave in which each end passes over two picks and then under two, with ends working alike in pairs across and along, is a
questions.explain: Hopsack is plain weave doubled in both directions.

questions.q: A warp rib shows ridges running
questions.explain: Each end passes over two or more picks together, so the ridges lie across the cloth.

questions.q: A herringbone is a twill that
options: Reverses direction with a break, so the lines do not meet point to point
questions.explain: The cut at the reversal gives the fish-bone look; a waved twill meets point to point instead.

questions.q: The draft of a weave shows
options: Which healds lift on each pick
Which heald frame carries each end
questions.explain: Ends that move identically are drawn on the same heald.

questions.q: The peg plan (lifting plan) shows
options: Which healds are lifted on each pick
How many ends go in each dent
questions.explain: It has one column per heald and one row per pick.

questions.q: Denting is the plan of how many ends are drawn through each dent of the reed.
questions.explain: Typical values are 2 for plain weave and 4 for a 4-end twill.

questions.q: A broken twill is one in which
options: The twill line is interrupted every few ends
questions.explain: Crow’s foot is a common broken twill.

questions.q: A 4-end “satinette” is used because no regular satin can be made on four ends.
questions.explain: The only moves available on 4 ends are 1 and 3, which give twills, and 2, which shares a factor with 4.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: Why the rules of move numbers, drafts and denting are what they are.

questions.q: Why can the move number of a satin not be 1?
options: The cloth would be too heavy
Successive interlacings would touch and form a twill line
It would need too many healds
The floats would be too long
questions.explain: A move of 1 (or repeat − 1) simply gives a twill.

questions.q: Which move numbers give a regular 8-end satin?
questions.explain: 3 and 5 share no factor with 8 and are not 1 or 7. The moves 2, 4 and 6 share a factor with 8.

questions.q: The number of heald frames a design needs equals
options: The number of different end movements
questions.explain: Ends that move alike share a heald, so only different movements need separate frames.

questions.q: For a straight draft, the peg plan is
options: The mirror image of the draft
questions.explain: With one end per heald in order, lifting the healds reproduces the design exactly.

questions.q: Why is a 3/1 twill usually dented 4 ends per dent?
options: So that each dent holds one whole repeat and its ends do not all lift together
Because the reed has four wires
questions.explain: Matching the dent to the repeat avoids reed marks.

questions.q: A 2/2 warp rib needs
questions.explain: There are only two different end movements, each lasting two picks.

questions.q: A pointed draft turns a straight 2/2 twill into
questions.explain: Threading forward and then back makes the diagonal turn at the point.

questions.q: A satin stripe looks darker or lighter than a sateen stripe of the same yarns because one shows mostly warp and the other mostly weft.
questions.explain: Warp and weft reflect light differently and often differ in colour, so the two faces contrast.

questions.q: Warp crimp is very high in a warp rib because
options: The warp bends over groups of thick or paired picks
questions.explain: The warp does all the bending while the weft lies nearly straight.

questions.q: A design with a 12-end repeat always needs 12 heald frames.
questions.explain: It needs only as many frames as there are different end movements, which may be far fewer.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting repeats, healds, floats and dents.

questions.q: How many ends are in the repeat of a regular satin with move numbers 3 or 5 and floats over 7 picks?
questions.explain: A 7/1 satin: 7 up + 1 down = 8 ends in the repeat.

questions.q: In one repeat of a 5-end sateen (5 × 5 squares), how many squares are filled on point paper?
questions.explain: Each end is up on only one pick: 5 ends × 1 = 5 filled squares.

questions.q: In a 5-end 4/1 satin, how many picks does each warp float pass over?
questions.explain: Each end is up for 4 picks and down for one.

questions.q: How many picks are in one repeat of a 2/2 warp rib (each end up for two picks, down for two)?
questions.explain: Up two, down two: 4 picks; the repeat is only 2 ends wide.

questions.q: How many ends and picks are in the repeat of a 3/3 hopsack? Enter the number of ends.
questions.explain: Three ends work together up, then three down: 6 ends (and 6 picks).

questions.q: A waved twill is drafted 1 2 3 4 5 6 5 4 3 2. How many healds does it use?
questions.explain: The highest heald number in the draft is 6.

questions.q: For that draft (1 2 3 4 5 6 5 4 3 2), how many ends are in the repeat?
questions.explain: Count the entries in the threading order: 10 ends.

questions.q: A cloth has 96 ends per inch in the reed, dented 4 per dent. How many dents per inch does the reed need?
questions.explain: 96 ÷ 4 = 24 dents per inch.

questions.q: A 5-end satin is dented 2 and 3 ends alternately. With 80 ends per inch in the reed, how many dents per inch are needed?
questions.explain: Average 2.5 ends per dent: 80 ÷ 2.5 = 32 dents per inch.

questions.q: How many valid move numbers has a 7-end satin (not 1, not 6, sharing no factor with 7)?
questions.explain: 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all valid: 4 move numbers.

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: A satin stripe from the designer’s sketch to the loom.

questions.q: How many ends are in one stripe repeat (one satin stripe plus one sateen stripe)?
How many picks are in the weave repeat?
questions.explain: Both weaves are on a 5-end base, so the repeat is 5 picks.

questions.q: How many heald frames are needed if every different end movement has its own frame?
questions.explain: Five different movements in the satin and five in the sateen: 10 frames.

questions.q: Which shedding mechanism suits this design?
questions.explain: Ten frames are more than a tappet’s 6–8 but well within a dobby’s range.

questions.q: On any one pick, how many of the 5 satin ends are lifted?
questions.explain: In a 4/1 satin each pick has four ends up and one down: 4.

questions.q: On any one pick, how many of the 10 ends of the stripe repeat are lifted in total?
questions.explain: Four of the satin ends and one of the sateen ends: 5.

questions.q: How many ends are in the full warp?
How many stripe repeats are there across the cloth?
questions.explain: 6,000 ends ÷ 10 = 600 repeats.

questions.q: If the whole warp were dented at an average of 2.5 ends per dent, how many dents per inch would the reed need?
questions.explain: 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40 dents per inch.

questions.q: The designer suggests move number 1 for the satin to “simplify” it. The result would be
options: A 4/1 twill with a clear diagonal, not a satin
questions.explain: A move of 1 lines the interlacings up into a twill; the scattered look of satin needs move 2 or 3 on five ends.

quizzes.case: A designer plans a satin-stripe shirting. Each stripe repeat has 5 ends of 4/1 satin beside 5 ends of 1/4 sateen, both on a 5-end base with move number 2. The cloth has 100 ends per inch in the reed and is 60 inches wide in the reed. The satin ends are dented 2 and 3 ends per dent alternately.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Mixed problems on weave construction and loom set-up.

questions.q: Which repeat size has NO regular satin?
questions.explain: On 6 ends, moves 2, 3 and 4 all share a factor with 6, and 1 and 5 give twills.

questions.q: A regular satin has 10 ends. How many valid move numbers does it have?
questions.explain: Only 3 and 7 share no factor with 10 (and are not 1 or 9): 2 move numbers.

questions.q: A stripe has 8 ends of 2/2 twill beside 8 ends of 2/2 hopsack. With suitable drafting the fewest healds needed are
questions.explain: The hopsack’s two movements (up two, down two, and the opposite) are the same as two of the twill’s four, so its ends can share those healds: 4 frames.

questions.q: A herringbone is drafted 1 2 3 4 | 2 1 4 3 (eight ends). How many heald frames does it need?
questions.explain: The second half reuses the same four movements, so 4 frames.

questions.q: A weft rib and a warp rib of the same yarns differ in that the weft rib
options: Has ridges running along the cloth and hides the warp
Cannot be woven on a tappet
questions.explain: In a weft rib the picks cover pairs of ends, the weft is on the surface and the ribs run warp-way.

questions.q: A 2/1 twill cloth has 90 ends per inch in the reed and is dented one repeat per dent. How many dents per inch are needed?
questions.explain: One repeat is 3 ends: 90 ÷ 3 = 30 dents per inch.

questions.q: A curved twill is made by changing the step of the twill gradually, so the line bends.
questions.explain: Steps such as 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 ends per pick make the diagonal steepen or flatten along its length.

questions.q: A dobby design is drawn with a pointed draft and its peg plan is a plain 2/2 twill. On the cloth you will see
questions.explain: The reversal is in the draft, so a simple twill lifting plan produces the waved effect.

questions.q: A 5-end satin stripe 2 inches wide is woven at 120 ends per inch. How many complete weave repeats are in the stripe?
questions.explain: 240 ends ÷ 5 = 48 repeats.

questions.q: Putting all four ends of a 3/1 twill repeat in one dent means that in every dent at least one end is down on each pick.
questions.explain: On each pick three ends of the repeat are up and one is down, so the dent never has all its ends lifting together.
